source_name: IFLR1000 — Montenegro jurisdiction and firm rankings
why_relevant: Directory that enumerates the Montenegrin firms ranked for banking & finance (Prelevic, JPM & Partners, Vujacic and others). Not commentary itself, but the authoritative shortlist of which advisory sites to monitor for client alerts.

Second, independent directory for actor mapping in a small market where the set of firms writing banking-regulatory commentary is only a dozen or so; also hosts country comparative guides written by local firms.

source_name: Law Office Vujacic (Podgorica) — practice areas / insights
why_relevant: Podgorica business-law firm that explicitly positions itself on liaison with the central bank and sector regulators for banks and financial institutions; a candidate publisher of Montenegrin-language client notes on new banking rules. Publication cadence unverified — monitor and downgrade if the site proves static.

source_name: Adzic & Partners (Podgorica) — leading Montenegrin business law firm site
why_relevant: Surfaced by the Montenegrin-language query for law firms tracking the Montenegrin legal framework; a domestic firm publishing in Montenegrin is exactly the bilingual, obligation-focused commentary this cell targets. Banking/payments specificity of output not yet confirmed.

source_name: Advokatska komora Crne Gore (Bar Association of Montenegro) — member directory
why_relevant: Official roster of admitted advocates and offices in Podgorica and other towns. Not commentary, but the exhaustive local-language actor list from which to identify small Montenegrin firms with banking practices that no international directory ranks.

source_name: PROPISI.NET Montenegro — consolidated Montenegrin legislation portal
why_relevant: Commercial legal-information publisher hosting consolidated texts of Montenegrin laws (incl. Zakon o platnom prometu) with amendment histories. Sits adjacent to this cell as the reference layer advisory alerts cite; useful for resolving which gazette number an alert is talking about.

English-language business outlet that translates Montenegrin regulatory change into operational consequences for banks and merchants (e.g. the July 2026 instant-payments switch and the pending Payment System Law amendments). Fills the gap where advisory firms have not yet published.

source_name: Crypto/CASP licensing advisory content on Montenegro (LegalBison, New Balkans Law Office and similar)
why_relevant: A visible commercial layer of advisory content aimed at inbound crypto/payments licensing in Montenegro, discussing the registration regime introduced by the 2025 AML amendments and MiCA/DORA/PSD2 spillover. Signals where regulatory arbitrage marketing is happening, but quality is uneven and some sites are SEO lead-generation rather than genuine practice.

source_name: Prelevic Law Firm (Podgorica) — banking & finance practice
why_relevant: Consistently top-ranked Montenegrin banking & finance firm; a priority candidate publisher of client alerts on CBCG rulebooks and payment-law changes. Listed here via its directory profile because the firm's own domain was not confirmed in this run — resolve the primary domain before scheduling collection.

Regional (Serbia-headquartered) firm with a Montenegro office and an established regional newsletter culture; likely to produce Montenegro-tagged banking/payments alerts. Firm's own publication URL not confirmed in this run.

source_name: Vijesti (vijesti.me) — daily newspaper / portal, Ekonomija section
why_relevant: Montenegro's most influential independent daily; historically the outlet that first reports CBCG supervisory measures, temporary administration, licence revocations (Atlas/IBM) and disputes over draft banking laws. Frequently co-publishes investigations with CIN-CG on suspicious transactions and correspondent-banking refusals.

source_name: Centar za istraživačko novinarstvo Crne Gore (CIN-CG)
why_relevant: The main Montenegrin investigative newsroom on financial crime: suspicious transactions, shell companies with 100m+ EUR turnover, correspondent banks refusing Montenegrin flows, crypto risk on an unregulated market. Surfaces supervisory failure signals well before any CBCG disclosure.

source_name: MANS — Mreža za afirmaciju nevladinog sektora
why_relevant: Anti-corruption NGO that both files FOI requests and publishes findings; a de facto media/pointer hybrid that reveals documents on state and regulatory institutions, and comments on draft laws. Useful for consultation disputes and for FOI-derived supervisory documents that media then amplify.

National news agency with a dedicated business wire (MINA-business). Agency copy is the upstream text most Montenegrin portals republish, so it gives the earliest, least-mutated version of CBCG and ministry statements, plus procedural updates such as Atlas bankruptcy claim lists.

source_name: RTCG — Radio Televizija Crne Gore, Ekonomija
why_relevant: National public broadcaster; carries official CBCG/ministry announcements, parliamentary committee coverage and stock-exchange items. Editorially cautious, so useful as a corroboration baseline against sharper private outlets.

Oldest Montenegrin daily (since 1944), with economy and crna hronika desks. Its crime desk is where prosecutions arising from bank failures and AML cases are reported, which links supervisory action to criminal process.

Opposition-leaning daily with a long record of adversarial coverage of the central bank and politically connected banks; carries allegations and leaked material that mainstream outlets treat more cautiously. Valuable as a weak-signal channel, requiring corroboration.
Montenegro's long-running independent weekly, historically strong on analytical pieces about the central bank, banking scandals and regulatory capture; longer-form context that daily reporting omits.
Established (2009) general news portal with an economy desk; carries ministry and CBCG announcements and political reaction to draft financial laws. Mid-tier corroboration source.
News portal with a distinct economy rubric and a browsable archive, useful for backfilling historical supervisory and consultation coverage rather than only live monitoring.

Local broadcaster that nonetheless republished the CBCG AML fines story in detail; illustrative of the local-broadcaster republication layer, which occasionally retains details trimmed from national coverage.

Carried the operational-deadline story on daily publication of blocked-company data following amendments to the Payment Transactions Law — the kind of implementation-date detail that matters for A3 deadline tracking and is easy to miss on official channels.

Mass-market portal that follows post-failure litigation and bankruptcy administration (Atlas bankruptcy trustee claims, related fund bankruptcies) — a strand of the resolution story that specialised finance media drop after the headline event.
Independent portal/radio; publishes economy pieces including analyses of the media market itself, and political-economy coverage relevant to lobbying around draft financial legislation.

Cross-border investigative network with a deep Montenegro bank file: First Bank ownership and criminal deposits, the special audit ordered by the central bank, and prosecutors dropping the probe into ~EUR 22m paid to privileged clients while a failed bank was under CBCG administration. The strongest English-language source on supervisory failure and non-enforcement.

English-language regional investigative coverage plus BIRN Montenegro's own reports on regulatory-agency transparency and spending, and on crypto regulation needing tougher rules. Bridges local-language findings into a form usable by non-Montenegrin analysts.

Emerging-markets business wire that covered the Atlas Banka conflict in English, including the bank owner's lawsuit against the president, the CBCG governor and the temporary administrator — i.e. the conflict dimension around supervisory action.
